report_title: Tortoiseshell / Imperial Kitten (Yellow Liderc / TA456 / Crimson Sandstorm) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: MITRE ATT&CK (group techniques enriched from named public reporting — see notes on the G0139 ID collision); Symantec/Broadcom 'Tortoiseshell Group Targets IT Providers in Saudi Arabia in Probable Supply Chain Attacks' (2019, https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/tortoiseshell-apt-supply-chain); CrowdStrike 'IMPERIAL KITTEN' adversary profile (2023, https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/adversaries/imperial-kitten/); PwC 'Yellow Liderc / IMAPLoader' strategic-web-compromise reporting (2023)

actor.name: Tortoiseshell
actor.mitre_canonical_name: Tortoiseshell (as tracked by MITRE ATT&CK on the public site; NOTE: the ATT&CK dataset bundled in this environment resolves the ID G0139 to 'TeamTNT', a cloud/container cryptomining group — the numeric ID is stale/reorganized in the local dataset and MUST NOT be used as the technique base; this pack is built from named Tortoiseshell/Imperial Kitten public reporting instead)
related_clusters: Overlaps and is frequently co-reported with CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN and PwC's Yellow Liderc; Microsoft tracks overlapping activity as Crimson Sandstorm (formerly Curium); TA456 is Proofpoint's tracking of the long-con fake-persona ('Marcella Flores') social-engineering operations. Some vendors caution that 'Tortoiseshell', 'Imperial Kitten', and 'Yellow Liderc' are convergent-but-not-identical clusters; attribution across the aliases is assessed at medium-high convergence, not proven single-entity identity.
actor.attribution: Iran-nexus; assessed to operate on behalf of the Iranian state with a suspected nexus to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Active since at least 2018 (Symantec, first Saudi IT-provider supply-chain wave) through 2024, per Symantec/Broadcom, CrowdStrike (IMPERIAL KITTEN) and PwC (Yellow Liderc).

key_campaigns.name: Saudi IT-provider supply-chain compromise
key_campaigns.summary: Compromised at least 11 organizations, majority in Saudi Arabia, focusing on IT providers to reach downstream customers via a trusted-relationship / supply-chain pivot. Deployed Backdoor.Syskit (a basic .NET/Delphi downloader-backdoor) plus publicly available and custom info-gathering tools (Sha.exe, Sha432.exe, stereoversioncontrol.exe, get-logon-history.ps1). Achieved domain-admin on at least two networks; several hundred hosts infected in some environments.

key_campaigns.name: IMPERIAL KITTEN social-engineering & malware operations
key_campaigns.summary: Job-recruitment-themed social engineering and fake personas used to deliver custom .NET implants; strategic web compromise (watering hole) and, in some intrusions, SQL injection of public-facing apps for initial access; publicly available tooling (ProcDump, NSSM, PAExec) alongside custom malware for credential theft and exfiltration against Middle East technology, logistics and IT targets, with heavy focus on Israel.

key_campaigns.name: Yellow Liderc / IMAPLoader watering-hole campaign
key_campaigns.summary: Strategic web compromises injecting bespoke JavaScript into legitimate (primarily Israel-related, maritime/shipping/logistics) websites to fingerprint visitors and exfiltrate host information to attacker-controlled domains, leading to deployment of IMAPLoader — a .NET malware that abuses IMAP email as its command-and-control channel and is delivered/loaded via HTA and DLL side-loading.

ttps.procedure_description: In the Yellow Liderc watering-hole operations, bespoke JavaScript injected into compromised legitimate websites fingerprints visiting hosts (browser, OS, configuration) and exfiltrates the profile to attacker-controlled infrastructure to select targets for follow-on IMAPLoader delivery.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — visitor fingerprinting executes in the browser on third-party compromised sites and is largely off victim-endpoint telemetry; hunt candidate via web-content integrity monitoring and outbound requests to newly-registered profiling domains

ttps.procedure_description: The injected profiling JavaScript enumerates browser/software attributes of visitors to compromised watering-hole sites to distinguish intended targets from incidental traffic.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — client-side software enumeration is not visible in victim server/endpoint logs; hunt candidate only

ttps.procedure_description: Registered domains for fake recruiting/job sites, fake-persona infrastructure, browser-profiling exfiltration endpoints, and C2.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim infrastructure acquisition is not endpoint-observable; intel/hunt candidate via lookalike-domain and registration monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Used attacker-controlled web services/domains to receive exfiltrated visitor-fingerprint data from watering-hole JavaScript.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim web-service acquisition; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Built elaborate long-con fake personas (e.g. the TA456 'Marcella Flores' persona) maintained over long periods to build rapport with targets before delivering malware.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — persona account creation is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate via persona and social-graph analysis

ttps.procedure_description: Created fake recruiter/social-media personas (LinkedIn/Facebook) to run job-recruitment-themed social engineering against targets.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — social-media persona creation is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Established email accounts used both for social-engineering correspondence and, for IMAPLoader, as mailbox infrastructure for IMAP-based command-and-control.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim mailbox creation; intel/hunt candidate (downstream IMAP C2 use is where detection lands, see T1071.003)

ttps.procedure_description: Developed custom malware including Backdoor.Syskit (in both Delphi and .NET) and the .NET IMAPLoader implant.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — capability development is not observable in victim telemetry; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Leveraged publicly available tools including ProcDump, NSSM, PAExec/PsExec and Mimikatz alongside custom implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tool acquisition is off-endpoint; downstream use is detectable — this entry is a hunt/intel candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Hosted malicious installers/payloads on fake recruiting and job-application websites designed to be delivered to targeted audiences.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — staging on adversary infrastructure is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate via lookalike-site and hosting monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Compromised legitimate (primarily Israel-related maritime/logistics) websites and injected bespoke JavaScript to stage strategic web compromises against their visitors.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — drive-by staging occurs on third-party sites; intel/hunt candidate via third-party web-content integrity monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Compromised IT/managed service providers (primarily in Saudi Arabia) as a stepping stone to reach their downstream customers — the defining Tortoiseshell tradecraft.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — upstream supply-chain compromise is largely outside a downstream victim's endpoint visibility; strategic intel/hunt candidate

ttps.technique_name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
ttps.procedure_description: Abused compromised IT-provider software/administration channels to distribute malware to downstream customer environments.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — software supply-chain compromise is upstream and hard to see from the victim; hunt candidate via unexpected provider-pushed binaries and integrity monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Exploited the trusted access that compromised IT/managed service providers already held into their customers' networks to gain initial access downstream.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — provider-originated access is detectable via anomalous third-party/remote-management logons and unexpected provider account activity, but requires baselining of legitimate provider behavior

ttps.procedure_description: Conducted strategic web compromises (watering holes) — injecting profiling JavaScript into legitimate sites and delivering payloads to selected visitors (Yellow Liderc / IMAPLoader).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the delivery occurs on third-party sites (off-victim), but the resulting browser-to-payload chain and outbound requests to profiling/staging domains are detectable via proxy and browser child-process telemetry on the victim endpoint

ttps.procedure_description: Used social-media/job-recruitment services (LinkedIn/Facebook fake personas) to deliver lures and links outside corporate mail controls.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — social-media-delivered lures bypass corporate mail gateways; user-awareness/hunt candidate with limited endpoint signal

ttps.procedure_description: In some IMPERIAL KITTEN intrusions used SQL injection against public-facing web applications to gain initial access.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — SQLi and web-app exploitation are detectable via WAF alerts, web-server error/anomaly logs and unexpected DB-to-shell process chains, but require web-tier instrumentation

ttps.procedure_description: Used stolen/legitimate credentials (harvested from compromised IT providers and via credential theft) to access downstream systems and move within victim networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — valid-account abuse is detectable via anomalous logon analytics (impossible travel, new host/time) but blends with legitimate use

ttps.procedure_description: Obtained domain-admin-level access on at least two compromised networks, then used those privileged domain accounts to broaden access (several hundred hosts infected in some environments).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — privileged domain-account use is detectable via anomalous admin-logon and privileged-group authentication analytics, but requires identity telemetry and good baselines

ttps.procedure_description: Executed PowerShell tooling including get-logon-history.ps1 for reconnaissance and used PowerShell to download and run payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — script-block/module logging and suspicious PowerShell parenting are core, well-covered detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: Ran commands and dropped/executed batch and staged executables (e.g. %Windir%\temp\bak.exe) via the Windows command shell.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — cmd.exe execution with anomalous parents and staged-binary paths (\Windows\Temp) is visible in process-creation logs

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttps.procedure_description: Used VBScript-based scripting/droppers in social-engineering delivery chains.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — wscript/cscript executing VBS, especially spawned by Office or archive extraction, is a strong detectable signal

ttps.procedure_description: Injected bespoke JavaScript into compromised watering-hole websites to fingerprint and target visitors.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the JavaScript runs in visitors' browsers on third-party sites; limited victim-endpoint signal; hunt candidate via web-content integrity monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Relied on targets clicking recruitment-themed links delivered via social media / fake personas to reach payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — malicious-link clicks are detectable via URL-gateway/proxy logs; endpoint signal is indirect

ttps.procedure_description: Relied on targets running malicious files (fake job-application installers / weaponized documents) to execute custom .NET implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — user-launched installers/documents spawning script or child processes is a core detectable behavior

ttps.procedure_description: Delivered/loaded IMAPLoader components via HTA files executed through mshta to proxy execution and evade defenses.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — mshta.exe executing HTA/remote content and spawning child processes is a rare LOLBin pattern with low false-positive rate

ttps.procedure_description: Used WMI for execution and remote command running during hands-on-keyboard activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — WMI process creation and WMI-Activity operational logs provide strong telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Created scheduled tasks to persist and execute payloads on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — scheduled-task creation is logged (Event ID 4698 / Task Scheduler operational) and highly detectable, especially with script/binary actions

ttps.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
ttps.procedure_description: Used NSSM (Non-Sucking Service Manager) to install malware as a Windows service for persistence.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — service creation (Event ID 7045 / 4697) and NSSM-registered services are strongly detectable

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttps.procedure_description: Used registry Run keys / startup locations for autostart persistence of implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Run-key writes are logged via registry-modification telemetry and are a well-covered persistence detection

ttps.technique_name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking
ttps.procedure_description: IMAPLoader is loaded via DLL side-loading / search-order hijacking of a legitimate signed host process.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — side-loading is detectable via unusual DLL loads from non-standard paths by signed binaries (image-load telemetry), but requires module-load logging and good baselines

ttps.procedure_description: Custom .NET implants used process injection to run in the context of legitimate processes.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — injection is detectable via EDR cross-process memory-write/thread-creation telemetry but generates volume that needs behavioral correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Loaded .NET payloads reflectively in memory (IMAPLoader / custom implants) to avoid writing the full payload to disk.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — in-memory .NET/reflective loading is detectable via CLR-load and AMSI/ETW telemetry but requires managed-runtime instrumentation

ttps.procedure_description: Obfuscated implant code and configuration to hinder analysis and detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — obfuscation is inferable from static/entropy analysis but needs dedicated inspection

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
ttps.procedure_description: Stored/transferred encrypted or encoded payloads and configuration to evade content inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — high-entropy/encoded payloads are detectable via file-entropy analytics but require dedicated scanning

ttps.procedure_description: Decoded/deobfuscated staged payloads at runtime (including via certutil in the Symantec-observed toolset).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'certutil -decode' and in-script decode routines are directly observable in command-line and script-block logging

ttps.procedure_description: Named payloads and staged binaries to blend in (e.g. bak.exe, sha.exe) and used recruitment-themed lures to appear legitimate.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — masquerading is detectable via name/path baselining and signature/content mismatch analysis

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: Staged executables in trusted-looking locations/names such as %Windir%\temp\bak.exe to reduce suspicion.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — legit-looking names in non-standard/temp paths are detectable via path/name baselining and signature mismatch

ttps.procedure_description: Modified registry values including HKLM\...\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Enablevmd and \Sendvmd during Syskit operations.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — registry modification is logged, but volume is high; value comes from watching the specific policy keys the actor sets

ttps.procedure_description: Deleted staged tools and payload artifacts after use to hinder investigation.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — file deletion is detectable via file-system audit / EDR delete events but is noisy and needs correlation with prior payload writes

ttps.procedure_description: Abused signed/side-loaded legitimate binaries to gain trust when loading IMAPLoader components.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — signature-trust abuse is detectable via certificate/thumbprint and load-path anomaly analytics on loaded binaries

ttps.procedure_description: Used ProcDump (and Mimikatz-style tooling) to dump LSASS memory for credential theft.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — process access to lsass.exe and ProcDump/Mimikatz signatures are highly observable in EDR and process-access telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Harvested credentials from local password stores using custom infostealers and public tools.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — password-store access is detectable mainly through known-tool execution and file/DPAPI-access telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttps.procedure_description: Stole credentials from web browsers as part of the infostealer collection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — access to browser Login Data stores is detectable via file-access and known-tool telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
ttps.procedure_description: Collected credentials stored in the Windows Credential Manager/vault.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Credential Manager/vault access is detectable via known-tool signatures and DPAPI/file-access telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Deployed keylogging capability within infostealer implants to capture typed credentials.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — keystroke-hooking APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Used fake login / recruitment web portals to capture credentials submitted by targets.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — credential harvesting occurs on attacker-hosted portals off the victim endpoint; hunt/intel candidate via phishing-page and domain monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Collected credentials stored in files across compromised hosts as part of infostealer activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — reading credential-bearing files leaves little discrete log signal; hunt candidate via file-access telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Ran systeminfo and used info-gathering tools to enumerate host details.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — systeminfo discovery is common; suspicious mainly in tight process-lineage/recon-burst context

ttps.procedure_description: Ran ipconfig and related commands to enumerate network configuration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 'ipconfig' is common but suspicious when clustered with other recon in a short process-lineage window

ttps.procedure_description: Ran whoami and get-logon-history.ps1 to enumerate the current user and prior logon history.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — whoami/logon-history enumeration is common; value is in process-lineage correlation and the distinctive get-logon-history.ps1 tool name

ttps.procedure_description: Enumerated running processes on compromised hosts via info-gathering tools.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — process enumeration is common but meaningful in recon-burst/process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: Enumerated local accounts using net.exe and info-gathering scripts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'net user'/'net localgroup' enumeration is directly observable in command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: Enumerated domain accounts and groups en route to domain-admin access.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'net user /domain' / 'net group /domain' enumeration is directly observable in command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: Enumerated local group membership to identify local administrators on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'net localgroup administrators' is directly observable in command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: Checked for installed security/AV software prior to deploying payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — security-software enumeration is detectable via command-line and process queries against AV services/registry, but is low-volume and needs targeted rules

ttps.procedure_description: Enumerated active network connections on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 'netstat' is common; meaningful in recon-burst/process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: Queried installed services on compromised hosts during hands-on activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — service enumeration is common; suspicious mainly in recon-burst/process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: Enumerated files and directories to locate credentials and data of interest.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — file/directory enumeration is high-volume and low-signal; hunt candidate via behavioral correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Used RDP to move laterally within compromised networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — RDP lateral movement is detectable via 4624 type-10 logons and internal-RDP fanout analytics

ttps.procedure_description: Used PAExec/PsExec over SMB admin shares to execute payloads on remote hosts and spread within networks (several hundred hosts infected in some environments).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — PsExec/PAExec service creation over admin shares (7045, 5145, remote service install) is strongly detectable

ttps.procedure_description: Captured screenshots of compromised desktops via infostealer capability.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — screen-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Collected files and data of interest from compromised local systems for exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — local collection is common; suspicious mainly via staging/archiving and upload command-lines in process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: Used infostealer implants to automatically collect credentials, browser data and host information.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — automated collection leaves little discrete log signal beyond the tool execution itself; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Staged collected data and tooling in temporary directories (e.g. %Windir%\temp) prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — local staging in temp is common and noisy; better as a hunt over file-write telemetry to \Windows\Temp

ttps.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
ttps.procedure_description: Archived collected data using utilities prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — archive-utility execution (rar/7z/zip) against staged data is detectable via process command-lines but needs correlation with prior collection

ttps.procedure_description: Used HTTP(S) web protocols for command-and-control and payload retrieval across Syskit and custom implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTTP C2 is detectable via proxy/beacon analytics and URI/JA3 anomalies but blends with normal web traffic

ttps.procedure_description: IMAPLoader uses IMAP email as its command-and-control channel — polling an attacker-controlled mailbox for commands and returning results by email, a signature Yellow Liderc / Imperial Kitten technique.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — IMAP/email-based C2 blends into normal mail traffic and its content is often encrypted; strong HUNT candidate via anomalous host-initiated IMAP to non-corporate mail providers, non-mail-client processes speaking IMAP, and beacon-like mailbox polling

ttps.procedure_description: Downloaded additional tools and payloads onto compromised hosts (Syskit is a downloader-backdoor; PowerShell/certutil also used to pull files).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — remote downloads via certutil/PowerShell and unexpected inbound file writes are strongly detectable in process + network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Encrypted C2 content (including within the IMAP mail-based channel) to defeat inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — symmetric-encrypted C2 content defeats content inspection; hunt on beacon/traffic-shape anomalies

ttps.procedure_description: Encoded C2 data (e.g. base64) within mail/web channels.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — base64-encoded C2 content is detectable via network inspection/encoding heuristics where TLS is absent

ttps.procedure_description: Routed C2 through intermediary infrastructure to obscure the true endpoints.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — proxy/relay use is inferred from network analysis; hunt candidate via connections to known-bad or anomalous intermediary infrastructure

ttps.procedure_description: Exfiltrated collected credentials and data back over the established C2 channel (including via the IMAPLoader mail channel).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — C2-channel exfil is detectable via outbound-volume anomalies on beaconing sessions, though the mail-based variant blends into normal mail flow

ttps.procedure_description: Watering-hole profiling JavaScript exfiltrated visitor host-fingerprint data to attacker-controlled web services/domains.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — browser-originated exfil to a web service from third-party sites is largely off victim-endpoint; hunt candidate via proxy telemetry to newly-registered profiling domains

detection_signals: Non-mail-client process initiating outbound IMAP (TCP 143/993) to a non-corporate/webmail provider, with beacon-like periodic mailbox polling (IMAPLoader mail-based C2)
mshta.exe executing an HTA (local or remote) that spawns script/child processes (IMAPLoader delivery)
Signed/legitimate binary loading an unexpected DLL from a non-standard/writable path (IMAPLoader DLL side-loading)
NSSM (nssm.exe) or sc.exe registering a new service pointing at a payload in a temp/user-writable path (Event ID 7045)
PAExec/PsExec service creation over SMB admin shares fanning out to many internal hosts (7045 / 5145)
ProcDump or comsvcs.dll MiniDump targeting lsass.exe; process access to lsass with dump-flag access masks
Execution of get-logon-history.ps1 or the named infostealers Sha.exe / Sha432.exe / stereoversioncontrol.exe / bak.exe (Symantec Tortoiseshell tooling)
certutil.exe with -decode / -urlcache, or PowerShell FromBase64String decoding staged payloads
Files written to %Windir%\temp\ such as rconfig.xml and bak.exe
Outbound connections to attacker profiling/staging domains from a browser process shortly after visiting a legitimate maritime/logistics site (watering-hole chain)
Provider/managed-service remote-management account performing anomalous logons or pushing unexpected binaries into a customer environment (supply-chain / trusted-relationship pivot)
Connections to the Symantec-reported C2 IPs 64.235.60.123 and 64.235.39.45
notes: IMPORTANT ID-COLLISION FINDING: the task base 'MITRE G0139 = Tortoiseshell' does NOT hold in this environment's bundled/reorganized ATT&CK dataset, where G0139 resolves to 'TeamTNT' (a cloud/container cryptomining group) and G1009 resolves to 'Moses Staff'. Basing a Tortoiseshell pack on the local G0139 technique list would have injected TeamTNT's cloud-miner TTPs (T1610/T1611/T1613/T1496.001/T1136.001 etc.) into an Iranian-espionage actor and poisoned every downstream pipeline stage. This pack therefore does NOT use the local G0139 technique array; it is built entirely from named public Tortoiseshell/Imperial Kitten/Yellow Liderc reporting (Symantec/Broadcom 2019, CrowdStrike IMPERIAL KITTEN 2023, PwC Yellow Liderc/IMAPLoader 2023) with each technique_id independently verified to exist in this environment's sigma-bundled ATT&CK dataset (all 57 verified True; one candidate, T1574.002, was dropped as absent — replaced by T1574.001 DLL Search-Order Hijacking, which is present and better matches IMAPLoader side-loading). TACTIC CONVENTIONS per the CI rules for this dataset: general defense-evasion techniques carry the tactic slug 'stealth' (T1218.005, T1055, T1620, T1027, T1027.013, T1140, T1036, T1036.005, T1112, T1070.004, T1553.002); no Impair-Defenses ('defense-impairment' T1685/T1686.x) technique is included because no public report credibly documents Tortoiseshell disabling AV/firewall — omitted rather than fabricated. All other tactics use canonical reconnaissance…exfiltration slugs. DETECTION vs HUNT routing hints are encoded in detection_feasibility: endpoint execution/persistence/credential-access lean DETECTION (mshta, NSSM service, PsExec fan-out, LSASS dump, scheduled task, net enumeration, certutil decode); the signature IMAP-based C2 (T1071.003), fake-persona/social-engineering resource-development, watering-hole browser fingerprinting/exfil, and supply-chain/trusted-relationship pivot lean HUNT (LOW feasibility). IOCs are conservative and sourced ONLY from the fetched Symantec/Broadcom report: 4 SHA256 hashes and 2 C2 IPs (64.235.60.123, 64.235.39.45). No domains/emails/CVEs are asserted because they were not present in a successfully-fetched primary source in this pass — the CrowdStrike adversary profile page and PwC report bodies were gated (profile landing page only; full IOC appendices behind gated reports), so IMAPLoader hashes/C2 mailbox domains should be ingested directly from those reports before being added. ATTRIBUTION is medium-high (Iran-nexus, suspected IRGC): the Tortoiseshell/Imperial Kitten/Yellow Liderc/TA456 aliases are convergent but not proven single-entity, so per pipeline rules the disagreement is preserved, not adjudicated. NO prompt-injection content was encountered in the fetched sources.
